ANALYSIS

[6] My role is to review all of the evidence and to determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.1
Appellants are credible

[7] The assessment of the appellants' credibility in the RPD's decision is problematic in many respects in addition to being based on elements peripheral to their claims. I did not consider it necessary to review the RPD's findings one by one, since some of them are peripheral to the point of not meriting discussion. Overall, I consider that the RPD's findings regarding fundamental aspects of the appellants' refugee protection claims are incorrect.

[8] The findings on which the RPD relied to cast doubt on the appellants' credibility are slim:
- In their BOC Form, the appellants do not indicate that the person who called the female appellant identified themselves as a CJNG member;
- According to the complaint to the Mexican Attorney General filed by the female appellant on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, and provided as evidence, the extortion attempts began with an initial call on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, not XXXX XXXX;
- According to the RPD, the female appellant testified that she had spoken only once with CJNG members, that is, during the call on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, and received text messages subsequently. Her complaint to the Mexican Attorney General indicates that a call was received on the day of the complaint, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. However, listening to the hearing reveals that the female appellant stated at the hearing that she had received an extortion call on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, and that the caller had again demanded XXXX XXXX XXXX pesos during this call;
- The male appellant testified that when he was approached by cartel members, it was the driver of the vehicle who pointed a gun at him. However, according to his complaint to the Mexican authorities concerning this event it was the passenger who pointed a gun at him;
- Since the RPD found that the appellants were not credible, it gave little weight to the documents provided as evidence.

[9] These elements are, in my view, insufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness, particularly since the appellants provided valid explanations for some of them at the hearing and since one of them is not well founded.

[10] In my opinion, the appellants' testimony was spontaneous, direct and consistent. They answered all questions and gave valid explanations for the issues that the RPD perceived in their testimony.

[11] In the absence of any inconsistencies, contradictions or omissions in the evidence or their testimony, I find that the appellants are credible.

[12] The RPD erred in assessing the male appellant's credibility.

[21] The appellants provided details regarding what led them to leave Mexico, and their testimony reveals escalating violence: the criminals attempted extortion, the appellants ignored them, and then the male appellant was threatened with a gun. At the hearing, the male appellant stated that his father was visited after they left, in XXXX 2019, and was asked where he was.5 Then, in early XXXX 2019, when the male appellant's father went to the appellants' apartment at their request to retrieve their belongings and clean it, he found a note (Exhibit D-6). The writer of the note indicates that the cartel knows that the appellants reported them and that from that point on whether or not they paid or the amount demanded was no longer important and that they were going to find them.6 Upon reading the note, the male appellant's father became frightened and left the apartment and has not returned there since that day.7 Lastly, in XXXX 2019, while the male appellant's father was driving his car, he escaped a murder attempt when someone in a vehicle shot at him8 (see Exhibit P-10). According to the appellants' amended BOC Form, the person who asked the male appellant's father in XXXX about his whereabouts was one of the assailants.

[22] When the RPD asked the male appellant what interest the cartel would have in leaving its area of influence to find them, he did not respond [translation] "in any way."9 He then explained that the cartel members had an interest in locating them because they had dared to report them. He added that they will not stop until they kill them and that this is what they tried to do to his father.10 Lastly, he testified that the CJNG has [translation] "connections" with other cartels and that it is impossible for them to move to another part of Mexico without being found.11

[23] In Maldonado,12 the Federal Court of Appeal held that when a refugee protection claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true, unless there are valid reasons to doubt them.

[24] Applying the presumption of truthfulness and considering the documentary evidence, I find the appellants' testimony to be credible, particularly with regard to their assertions that they would not be safe in Mexico.

[25] In my opinion, the CJNG's interest in locating the appellants goes beyond mere financial gain. As the male appellant stated at the hearing, they defied the cartel by reporting them. Given that the male appellant's father was contacted and attacked and that the CJNG members were looking for them, it can be concluded that the persons whom the appellants fear have the motivation and the means to locate them. The fact that the male appellant can identify the persons who threatened him is another reason potentially motivating the cartels to track them down.

[26] Even if the cartel's interest were purely financial, the documentary evidence indicates that an outstanding debt could motivate the cartel to track someone outside their area of influence.13

[29] According to the documents concerning country conditions in the NDP on Mexico of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, there is a high and growing level of violence in Mexico, criminal activities are generally carried out with impunity and criminal organizations often collude with corrupt police and local and state government authorities.15

[30] With regard to the CJNG specifically, it is difficult for me to imagine the existence of a viable IFA in Mexico against this cartel when the motivation to track the refugee protection claimants has been established. The reasons for this are as follows.

[31] According to a recent study by the United States Library of Congress, the CJNG is expanding in Mexico and is one of the largest and most violent cartels.16 The same document indicates that the Mexican government declared the CJNG one of the most dangerous cartels in Mexico and one of the two with the broadest reach:
In 2015, the Mexican government declared CJNG one of the most dangerous cartels in the country and one of two with the most extensive reach. In October 2016, the U.S. Department of the Treasury echoed the Mexican government when it described the group as one of the world's "most prolific and violent drug trafficking organizations." According to some analysts, CJNG has operations throughout the Americas, Asia, and Europe. The group allegedly is responsible for distributing cocaine and methamphetamine along "10,000 kilometres of the Pacific Coast in a route that extends from the Southern Cone to the border of the United States and Canada."
To best understand CJNG's international reach, it is important to first consider its expansion within Mexico. In 2016, many analysts maintained the cartel had presence throughout the country in a combined area that made up nearly half of Mexico. Recent reports indicate the group has pushed further into Aguas Calientes, San Luis Potosi, and Zacatecas states. The group has battled Los Zetas and Gulf Cartel factions in Tabasco, Veracruz, and Guanajuato, and it has battled the Sinaloa federation in the Baja peninsulas and Chihuahua. CJNG's ambitious expansion campaign has led to high levels of violence, particularly in Ciudad Juarez and Tijuana, where it has clashed with the Sinaloa federation for control of the lucrative heroin trade and corresponding smuggling routes. The group has also been linked to several mass graves in southwestern Mexico and was responsible for shooting down an army helicopter in 2015, the first successful takedown of a military asset of its kind in Mexico.17

According to analysts, the CJNG is either present through alliances or a clear challenger for leadership of organized crime throughout Mexico.21 The documentary evidence indicates that criminal organizations have the means to track individuals outside their areas of operation, including through temporary alliances with other groups.22 Lastly, a number of analysts are of the opinion that the CJNG's reach extends beyond Mexico, since it is involved in activities throughout the Americas as well as Asia and Europe.23

[33] The evidence also shows that the cartels often collude with corrupt police and local and state government authorities.24 A recent study indicates that the CJNG is sufficiently powerful to corrupt and even challenge the Mexican state with complete impunity.25 The same document reports that the CJNG is involved in large-scale corruption. For example, one source reports that half the Guadalajara police force is on the CJNG's payroll.26

[34] The documentary evidence also confirms the male appellant's testimony to the effect that criminal organizations have access to police databases. Additionally, the evidence shows that it is possible for cartels to purchase lists of private personal information, including addresses.27 Multiple sources report collusion between the Mexican authorities and the cartels and cite, for example, a case in which police arrested youths belonging to a rival cartel of the CJNG and turned them over to it. These persons were subsequently executed by the CJNG.28

[35] In light of the facts and the documentary evidence, and insofar as the agents of harm were aware that the appellants had filed reports with the police, I am of the view that, on a balance of probabilities, the CJNG cartel would have the motivation and the means to track the appellants in Mexico.

[36] In my opinion, on a balance of probabilities, this possibility continues to exist, because the CJNG still has the means to track the appellants and the motivation to do so, since its reputation depends in part on its capacity to make those who refuse to cooperate with the cartel disappear.29

[37] Applying the presumption of truthfulness and considering the documentary evidence, I find the appellants' testimony to be credible, particularly with regard to their assertion that they would in danger everywhere in Mexico.

[38] Consequently, on a balance of probabilities, there is a serious possibility that the appellants would be subjected to a risk to their lives, to a danger of torture or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Mexico.
Appellants do not have adequate state protection

[39] Although states are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens, I consider that the appellants do not have access to adequate protection from the Mexican state.

[40] The appellants attempted twice to file a police complaint. Both times, the cartel was informed of these complaints, and the appellants suffered the consequences. During their testimony, the appellants indicated that they did not feel safe in Mexico because of the collusion between criminals and the police. The appellants left Mexico because they considered that the state authorities would be unable to protect them from the persons extorting money from them whom they had tried to report to the police.

[41] The objective documentary evidence confirms that the Mexican state authorities frequently collude with criminal groups.

REASONS FOR DECISION
[1] I am allowing the appeal.

[2] The appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Mexico. The appellants assert that they were threatened by the Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generacion (CJNG) in an effort to extort money from them, and that they fear being killed by that group because they did not meet their demands.

[3] In early XXXX 2019, the female appellant received extortion calls and text messages after making a large deposit in a bank account. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, she received a text message threatening her and demanding XXXX XXXX XXXX pesos, followed by a second message threatening her husband's life. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, the female appellant reported the financial extortion and threats to the public ministry. She was allegedly advised to ignore these messages and to change telephone numbers. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, the male appellant was threatened by two men in a car who ordered him to pay the amount demanded or else he would be killed and the female appellant abducted. The appellants were afraid and made the decision to leave their country on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. They resigned from their jobs the next day. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, they submitted a second complaint to the prosecutor's office and left Mexico. After they left, the male appellant's father found threats at their former residence. The male appellant's father himself was attacked by CJNG members who were allegedly still looking for the appellants.

[4] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the appellants were not credible due to omissions and contradictions that it identified between their testimony, the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) and the documents submitted in evidence.
ANALYSIS

[6] My role is to review all of the evidence and to determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.1
Appellants are credible

[7] The assessment of the appellants' credibility in the RPD's decision is problematic in many respects in addition to being based on elements peripheral to their claims. I did not consider it necessary to review the RPD's findings one by one, since some of them are peripheral to the point of not meriting discussion. Overall, I consider that the RPD's findings regarding fundamental aspects of the appellants' refugee protection claims are incorrect.

[9] These elements are, in my view, insufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness, particularly since the appellants provided valid explanations for some of them at the hearing and since one of them is not well founded.
[10] In my opinion, the appellants' testimony was spontaneous, direct and consistent. They answered all questions and gave valid explanations for the issues that the RPD perceived in their testimony.
[11] In the absence of any inconsistencies, contradictions or omissions in the evidence or their testimony, I find that the appellants are credible.

[12] The RPD erred in assessing the male appellant's credibility.
Appellants are subjected personally to a risk to their lives in Mexico
[13] The appellants demonstrated that they are subjected personally to a risk to their lives that is not faced generally by other Mexican nationals under subsection 97(1).

[14] The appellants were targeted, personally and specifically, by death threats. The male appellant was tracked down and threatened with a gun. These risks to life are, due to their nature and intensity, different from the risk faced generally by other Mexican nationals. I conclude that it is more likely than not that the appellants are subjected personally to a risk to their lives not faced generally by other Mexican nationals.
Appellants have no internal flight alternative in Mexico
[15] The RPD did not express an opinion as to the viability of an internal flight alternative (IFA) for the appellants in Mexico. However, it questioned the appellants in this regard at the hearing.2
[16] The legal test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged.3

[17] Under the first prong of the test, I must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the appellants are not subjected personally to a risk to their lives, to a danger of torture or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in a part of Mexico.
[18] Under the second prong of the test, the conditions of the IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in light of all the circumstances, for the appellants to seek refuge there.

[19] For the following reasons, I am of the opinion that the first prong of the legal test for an IFA has not been met.
Motivation to locate appellants

[20] At the hearing, the appellants testified that they did not feel safe in Mexico. They explained a number of times why they considered that the criminals who threatened them could easily track them down anywhere in Mexico.4

[21] The appellants provided details regarding what led them to leave Mexico, and their testimony reveals escalating violence: the criminals attempted extortion, the appellants ignored them, and then the male appellant was threatened with a gun. At the hearing, the male appellant stated that his father was visited after they left, in XXXX 2019, and was asked where he was.5 Then, in early XXXX 2019, when the male appellant's father went to the appellants' apartment at their request to retrieve their belongings and clean it, he found a note (Exhibit D-6). The writer of the note indicates that the cartel knows that the appellants reported them and that from that point on whether or not they paid or the amount demanded was no longer important and that they were going to find them.6 Upon reading the note, the male appellant's father became frightened and left the apartment and has not returned there since that day.7 Lastly, in XXXX 2019, while the male appellant's father was driving his car, he escaped a murder attempt when someone in a vehicle shot at him8 (see Exhibit P-10). According to the appellants' amended BOC Form, the person who asked the male appellant's father in XXXX about his whereabouts was one of the assailants.

[22] When the RPD asked the male appellant what interest the cartel would have in leaving its area of influence to find them, he did not respond [translation] "in any way."9 He then explained that the cartel members had an interest in locating them because they had dared to report them. He added that they will not stop until they kill them and that this is what they tried to do to his father.10 Lastly, he testified that the CJNG has [translation] "connections" with other cartels and that it is impossible for them to move to another part of Mexico without being found.11

[23] In Maldonado,12 the Federal Court of Appeal held that when a refugee protection claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true, unless there are valid reasons to doubt them.

[24] Applying the presumption of truthfulness and considering the documentary evidence, I find the appellants' testimony to be credible, particularly with regard to their assertions that they would not be safe in Mexico.

[25] In my opinion, the CJNG's interest in locating the appellants goes beyond mere financial gain. As the male appellant stated at the hearing, they defied the cartel by reporting them. Given that the male appellant's father was contacted and attacked and that the CJNG members were looking for them, it can be concluded that the persons whom the appellants fear have the motivation and the means to locate them. The fact that the male appellant can identify the persons who threatened him is another reason potentially motivating the cartels to track them down.

[26] Even if the cartel's interest were purely financial, the documentary evidence indicates that an outstanding debt could motivate the cartel to track someone outside their area of influence.13
Means to locate appellants
[27] The appellants argue that the documentary evidence confirms the CJNG's presence in Mexico as well as the danger it poses and its [translation] "reach."

[28] When asked at the hearing whether he would be able to live safely in Mérida or Campeche, the male appellant stated that he would not and that the CJNG already had all the information it needed to track the appellants down in Mexico.14

[29] According to the documents concerning country conditions in the NDP on Mexico of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, there is a high and growing level of violence in Mexico, criminal activities are generally carried out with impunity and criminal organizations often collude with corrupt police and local and state government authorities.15

[30] With regard to the CJNG specifically, it is difficult for me to imagine the existence of a viable IFA in Mexico against this cartel when the motivation to track the refugee protection claimants has been established. The reasons for this are as follows.

[31] According to a recent study by the United States Library of Congress, the CJNG is expanding in Mexico and is one of the largest and most violent cartels.16 The same document indicates that the Mexican government declared the CJNG one of the most dangerous cartels in Mexico and one of the two with the broadest reach:
In 2015, the Mexican government declared CJNG one of the most dangerous cartels in the country and one of two with the most extensive reach. In October 2016, the U.S. Department of the Treasury echoed the Mexican government when it described the group as one of the world's "most prolific and violent drug trafficking organizations." According to some analysts, CJNG has operations throughout the Americas, Asia, and Europe. The group allegedly is responsible for distributing cocaine and methamphetamine along "10,000 kilometres of the Pacific Coast in a route that extends from the Southern Cone to the border of the United States and Canada."
To best understand CJNG's international reach, it is important to first consider its expansion within Mexico. In 2016, many analysts maintained the cartel had presence throughout the country in a combined area that made up nearly half of Mexico. Recent reports indicate the group has pushed further into Aguas Calientes, San Luis Potosi, and Zacatecas states. The group has battled Los Zetas and Gulf Cartel factions in Tabasco, Veracruz, and Guanajuato, and it has battled the Sinaloa federation in the Baja peninsulas and Chihuahua. CJNG's ambitious expansion campaign has led to high levels of violence, particularly in Ciudad Juarez and Tijuana, where it has clashed with the Sinaloa federation for control of the lucrative heroin trade and corresponding smuggling routes. The group has also been linked to several mass graves in southwestern Mexico and was responsible for shooting down an army helicopter in 2015, the first successful takedown of a military asset of its kind in Mexico.17

[32] According to the documentary evidence, the CJNG is one of the largest and most dangerous cartels in Mexico18 and controls half of Mexico.19 The evidence also shows that the CJNG is active in 24 of Mexico's 32 states but that, through alliances (with the Familia Michoacana20 cartel among others) or small group cells, it is present in all 32 Mexican states. According to analysts, the CJNG is either present through alliances or a clear challenger for leadership of organized crime throughout Mexico.21 The documentary evidence indicates that criminal organizations have the means to track individuals outside their areas of operation, including through temporary alliances with other groups.22 Lastly, a number of analysts are of the opinion that the CJNG's reach extends beyond Mexico, since it is involved in activities throughout the Americas as well as Asia and Europe.23

[33] The evidence also shows that the cartels often collude with corrupt police and local and state government authorities.24 A recent study indicates that the CJNG is sufficiently powerful to corrupt and even challenge the Mexican state with complete impunity.25 The same document reports that the CJNG is involved in large-scale corruption. For example, one source reports that half the Guadalajara police force is on the CJNG's payroll.26

[34] The documentary evidence also confirms the male appellant's testimony to the effect that criminal organizations have access to police databases. Additionally, the evidence shows that it is possible for cartels to purchase lists of private personal information, including addresses.27 Multiple sources report collusion between the Mexican authorities and the cartels and cite, for example, a case in which police arrested youths belonging to a rival cartel of the CJNG and turned them over to it. These persons were subsequently executed by the CJNG.28

[35] In light of the facts and the documentary evidence, and insofar as the agents of harm were aware that the appellants had filed reports with the police, I am of the view that, on a balance of probabilities, the CJNG cartel would have the motivation and the means to track the appellants in Mexico.

[36] In my opinion, on a balance of probabilities, this possibility continues to exist, because the CJNG still has the means to track the appellants and the motivation to do so, since its reputation depends in part on its capacity to make those who refuse to cooperate with the cartel disappear.29

[37] Applying the presumption of truthfulness and considering the documentary evidence, I find the appellants' testimony to be credible, particularly with regard to their assertion that they would in danger everywhere in Mexico.

[38] Consequently, on a balance of probabilities, there is a serious possibility that the appellants would be subjected to a risk to their lives, to a danger of torture or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Mexico.
Appellants do not have adequate state protection
[39] Although states are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens, I consider that the appellants do not have access to adequate protection from the Mexican state.

[40] The appellants attempted twice to file a police complaint. Both times, the cartel was informed of these complaints, and the appellants suffered the consequences. During their testimony, the appellants indicated that they did not feel safe in Mexico because of the collusion between criminals and the police. The appellants left Mexico because they considered that the state authorities would be unable to protect them from the persons extorting money from them whom they had tried to report to the police.
[41] The objective documentary evidence confirms that the Mexican state authorities frequently collude with criminal groups.

[42] According to the most recent version of the NDP on Mexico, impunity and low prosecution rates remain significant problems in Mexico. The most recent report from the United States Department of State indicates that the involvement of illegal groups in unlawful or arbitrary killings, forced disappearance and torture, and arbitrary detention, sometimes in collaboration with government institutions, is still a major human rights issue.30 The Department of State notes further that impunity for human rights abuses remains a problem, with "extremely low rates of prosecution for all crimes."31 In fact, the Mexican government's federal statistics agency estimates that "94 percent of crimes [are] either unreported or not investigated."32 According to Open Society Foundations, Mexico is experiencing a "crisis of atrocity and impunity"33 and is one of the most corrupt countries, with the highest impunity, in the Americas.34

[43] The documentary evidence shows that the police have been involved in kidnappings and extortion and have both protected and acted directly on behalf of organized crime in Mexico. The evidence demonstrates the involvement of the police, army and other state agents, sometimes in coordination with criminal organizations, in arbitrary killings, forced disappearance, torture and arbitrary detention by the government and illegal armed groups.35

[44] Lastly, the documentary evidence also indicates that the security forces themselves continue to carry out extrajudicial executions, forced disappearance and torture in Mexico. Impunity for such crimes remains the norm, particularly when they are committed by law enforcement. The evidence shows that prosecutors and police routinely neglect to take basic investigative steps to identify those responsible for enforced disappearances, often telling the missing people's families to investigate on their own.36
[45] I consider that the appellants' testimony and the documentary evidence are sufficient to rebut the presumption of state protection.
CONCLUSION

[46] The appeal is allowed. I substitute the determination of the RPD with my own determination that the appellants are refugees persons in need of protection.
